newsitem.title: USA: Jack Kemp -- more happy warrior than attack dog.
newsitem.headline: Jack Kemp -- more happy warrior than attack dog.

text.p: Republicans who used to say Bob Dole was too nasty now say Jack Kemp is too nice.

That is about the only gripe heard concerning the burly, silver-haired conservative with the passion for tax cutting as he concludes a stint as Dole's vice presidential running mate and awaits the verdict of the voters next Tuesday.

Many fellow Republicans had hoped Kemp would function as the ticket's attack dog -- as Dole himself did when he was President Gerald Ford's running mate 20 years ago -- and rip into Democratic opponents Bill Clinton and Al Gore.
That is not the style of the genial former professional football star, congressman and White House Cabinet secretary.

True Kemp, 61, has been a hard-nosed competitor since his gridiron quarterback days with the Buffalo Bills and San Diego Chargers 30 years ago. And he could be a dogged ideologue for pro-growth tax-cut policies many (including Dole) felt extreme when he was a congressman from New York in the 1970s and '80s.
But he was never mean, always a chatty persuader ready to bend the ears of opponents he called his friends.

That continued after he left Congress in 1989 and became Housing Secretary under President George Bush, and on into the 1996 campaign where he worked especially hard to woo usually Democratic constitutencies -- blacks, Hispanics and the poor -- to the Republican side.
The courtly side that rankled some Republicans was evident in his televised Oct. 9 debate with Vice President Gore.
It was a contest of two bookworms on policy issues, in which Kemp came across as even more professorial than the notoriously stolid Gore, and shunned two-fisted attacks.
Most viewers told pollsters they thought Gore won.

Nonetheless, Kemp has been a tireless campaigner and performed one duty few Republicans could have, venturing into inner-city ghettos like New York's Harlem to argue that the key to upward mobility lies in the venture capitalism espoused by his party.

His affinity for minority groups is a product of the athlete's life that was his as a young man. His theories of promoting inner city economic resurgence were refined during his years as U.S. housing secretary.
He also contributed to Dole's cause by helping to offset worries about the Kansan's advancing age of 73.
Kemp, fit and usually tanned, is an energetic and youthful 61, given to bounding up stage stairs two at a time, vigorous rounds of handshaking and tossing footballs with fans.

Dole's choice of Kemp surprised many, since the two were not close and had clashed often on policy. Dole was a lifelong budget-balancing devotee opposed to unfinanced tax cuts. Kemp saw tax cutting as the priority goal indispensable to growth.
But Dole this year shifted his stance in order to make the promise of a 15 percent tax cut the heart of his campaign.
The two appeared friendly in join campaign appearances.

Kemp was born on July 13, 1935, in Los Angeles. He attended Occidental College in California and parlayed his football-playing experience there into a pro career that peaked when he led Buffalo to the championship of the American Football League -- now defunct -- twice in the mid-sixties.

He retired from football after the 1969 season and turned his celebrity to political use, representing Buffalo in the House of Representatives for 18 years. After a stint in Bush's Cabinet, he pursued a lucrative career on the lecture circuit and as co-director of the Empower America think-tank.
He and his wife Joanne live in the Washington suburb of Bethesda, Maryland. They have four grown children -- Jeffrey, Jennifer, Judith and James -- and 11 grandchildren.
